\section{Bureau Visibility and Affordability Screening}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Every number is read from thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex (results/raw/rq3s.parquet,
% 100 replicates per arm), tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, or from
% results/summary/results_numbers.json, all generated by notebooks/scripts/build_results_tables.py.

This section answers RQ3. The benchmark is the position before the reporting arrangements.
Under bureau visibility, \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's
Regulation 23A test, which is how we model the reported bureau arrangements
\citep{businessday_bnpl_2026}. Under mandatory screening, the same test is applied to every
\ac{BNPL} request, a stricter version of the \ac{FCA}'s affordability check
\citep{fca_ps26_1,woolard2021}. Regulation 23A excludes incidental credit
\citep[reg.~23A(2)(e)]{sa_ncr_affordability_2015}, which \ac{BNPL} may become
(Section~\ref{sec:background}), so screening is a policy analogue. A third arm combines both
switches (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}). Each arm runs at $\beta=0$ and $\beta=0.3$ with one hundred replicates on shared seeds, so a
difference of 0.13 points in default is detected about half the time.
% switch_se_max = 0.00065 in results_numbers.json; 2 x 0.065 = 0.13.

The two switches move default in opposite directions (Table~\ref{tab:scenarios};
Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios}). Bureau visibility raises it by $0.20 \pm 0.07$ points at $\beta=0$,
and by $0.19 \pm 0.07$ among households whose income covers food and rent.
% 0.19 +/- 0.07: rq3s_bureau_diff_contestable_b0 (+ _se), results/summary/contestable_default.json.
At $\beta=0.3$ the rise, $0.10 \pm 0.06$, is not detectable, and the two estimates do not differ
detectably ($-0.09 \pm 0.08$ points). Screening lowers default by
$0.93 \pm 0.06$ points at $\beta=0$ and $1.03 \pm 0.06$ at $\beta=0.3$. As in
Section~\ref{sec:results-injection}, the table's 90+ row is not used for effects.
% -0.09 +/- 0.08: switch_bureau_interaction (+ _se), results/summary/results_numbers.json.

Visibility can only add obligations to the test, so the lender refuses about 13\% more
applications and lends 12 to 15\% less. Arrears and late fees are 9.9\% of the obligation it
sees at application. A quarter is on agreements opened in the same tick against the same
shortfall, which we assume a bureau reporting with a lag would not show, so the switch
overstates what a lender sees.
% arrears_share_at_application (0.099) and live_opened_same_tick_share_at_application (0.25) for
% beta0.all in results/summary/bureau_visible_split.json (notebooks/scripts/check_bureau_visible_split.py,
% seeds 80,000-80,019). 13%: +124/954 and +121/954; 12 to 15%: lever_bureau_beta{0,0.3}_lending_diff
% over lever_bench_beta{0,0.3}_lending (-0.119, -0.150).
A refused household in the model has no other source of credit, so the debt service it cannot
meet becomes arrears, and the food and rent that the loan would have paid go unpaid. At
$\beta=0$ the share of households short of food and rent in a tick rises by $0.125 \pm 0.016$
points and the share ever short by $0.091 \pm 0.024$ (Table~\ref{tab:scenarios-distress}).
Default rises detectably in Q1 and Q3 at $\beta=0$, by $0.17 \pm 0.08$ and
$0.43 \pm 0.13$ points, and in no quintile at $\beta=0.3$. If these ten quintile comparisons
were independent, chance would make two or more detectable about 7\% of the time.
\ac{BNPL} volume falls by only 1.3 to 1.5\%, because the switch acts on traditional lending.
% Q1 at beta = 0 is 0.169 +/- 0.080 unrounded (2.12 SE). 7%: P(2 or more of 10) at p = 0.0455,
% 1 - 0.9545^10 - 10(0.0455)(0.9545^9) = 0.073. The quintiles and both betas share seeds 80,000-80,099.

The model's rules favour a rise in default under visibility. A refusal can put a household into
arrears at once, whereas a granted loan is repaid over 25 months, partly after the run ends.
The switches were not run under the other rules of Table~\ref{tab:effect} or over a longer horizon, so the result gives the sign of
the affordability channel in the model within two years and is not a forecast.

Almost all of screening's fall in default is in Q1, $-4.68 \pm 0.10$ points at $\beta=0$ and
$-4.70 \pm 0.10$ at $\beta=0.3$, against a \ac{BNPL} effect in Q1 of about four points
(Section~\ref{sec:results-distribution}). A refused shortfall request passes in full to the
traditional lender (Algorithm~\ref{alg:gate}), which applies the same test, and the lender's
refusals rise by 1{,}827, close to their level without \ac{BNPL} (Table~\ref{tab:baseline-arms}).
The offset is therefore close to mechanical. Screening applies to \ac{BNPL} requests the same test
that already keeps these households from the lender
(Section~\ref{sec:results-injection}). It lowers default by about as much as \ac{BNPL} raises it,
while holding falls by 0.3 points at $\beta=0$ and 0.7 at $\beta=0.3$ and volume by about 3\%.
Default under screening, 20.88\% at $\beta=0$ including the starting stock, is close to the
baseline's 20.73\% on other seeds. Screening leaves more households short of food and rent: at
$\beta=0$ the share short in a tick rises by $0.036 \pm 0.015$ points and the share ever short by
$0.055 \pm 0.027$, both just detectable, and at $\beta=0.3$ neither change is detectable. The runs
record no Rand amount unpaid, so the fall in default does not show that households
are better off.
% lever_afford_beta0_default (results_numbers.json); baseline_default (seeds 10,000-10,019).
% Food and rent: scen_{bureau,afford}_beta{0,0.3}_cdist_{tick,ever}_diff (+ _se),
% results_numbers.json; tab_scenarios_distress.

With both switches, default is $0.90 \pm 0.05$ points below the benchmark at $\beta=0$ and
$0.85 \pm 0.05$ at $\beta=0.3$. Adding screening to visibility lowers default by
$1.09 \pm 0.07$ points at $\beta=0$. Adding visibility to screening changes it by
$+0.04 \pm 0.05$ points at $\beta=0$ and raises it by $0.18 \pm 0.06$ at $\beta=0.3$. Peer
influence does not detectably change the benchmark or the effect of either switch.
% switch_both_less_bureau_beta0, switch_both_less_afford_beta{0,0.3}, switch_bench_beta_gap,
% switch_bureau_interaction and switch_afford_interaction (+ _se), results/summary/results_numbers.json.

Two further levers, a cooling-off window on want-driven purchases and
a hypothetical cap on platforms owed, are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:levers}. None of their
fourteen contrasts with the benchmark, which share the benchmark arm at each $\beta$, is
detectable, although the window removes up to 40.5\% of \ac{BNPL} volume at $\beta=0.3$ and a
cap of one platform removes 35 to 40\%. The window does not act on borrowing for a shortfall,
which is where the \ac{BNPL} effect arises.
% 40.5%: four-tick window at beta = 0.3; 35 to 40%: cap of one (35.1 and 40.3), tab_cooloff and tab_cap.

\subsection{Answer to RQ3}
\label{sec:scenarios-answer}

Bureau visibility raises the traditional lender's refusals by about 13\% and default by
$0.20 \pm 0.07$ points at $\beta=0$, since in the model a refused household has no other source of credit. At $\beta=0.3$ the rise is not detectable, but the two estimates
do not differ detectably. Mandatory screening lowers default by 0.93 to 1.03 points, almost all
in the poorest quintile, about as much as \ac{BNPL} adds, because it applies the lender's test to
\ac{BNPL}. At $\beta=0$ both switches
raise the share of households short of food and rent, and at $\beta=0.3$ only visibility
does. Visibility therefore worsens both measures at $\beta=0$, and whether screening leaves households
better off is open.
